text: Kubernetes stacks three objects on top of each other to run your application, and it's worth knowing exactly why each layer exists instead of treating it as boilerplate you copy and paste. This lesson walks the real parent-child chain from a single Pod all the way up to a Deployment, and shows you how to read that relationship directly with kubectl.

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers scheduled together on the same node, sharing a network namespace. Apply a bare Pod like this one and you get exactly one running container, with no self-healing at all. If its node fails, the Pod dies with it and nothing brings it back.

A ReplicaSet fills that gap by reconciling count: how many Pods matching its label selector currently exist, versus how many should. A Deployment then sits above the ReplicaSet to reconcile change over time — when you update the Pod template, it creates a brand-new ReplicaSet and shifts replicas across gradually, which a bare ReplicaSet can never do on its own.

You can prove the ReplicaSet's self-healing loop yourself: delete one Pod by name, and a replacement appears within seconds, with a new random suffix. The ReplicaSet never noticed which Pod was removed — only that the count dropped from three to two, and it acted to fix exactly that.

kubectl get deployments, replicasets, and pods together tell the whole story in their names. The Deployment web-app creates a ReplicaSet named after a hash of its Pod template, and that ReplicaSet creates Pods named after itself plus a random suffix. Run kubectl describe pod and the Controlled By field names that ReplicaSet directly — nothing in this chain is hidden.

Decide the count, decide the change, run the containers — three layers, each with one distinct job, and none of it hidden from you if you know which kubectl command to run. Next lesson moves to a different problem entirely: getting configuration and credentials out of your container image using ConfigMaps and Secrets.
